item.title: Bridging Bilingual Pedagogy and Sports Science: An EMI Classroom Observation / 雙語教學與運動科學的交會：EMI 課程觀課紀錄
item.description:
延續 ASU 的教學基石 (Continuing the ASU Pedagogical Foundation)

It was a distinct privilege to welcome Alexis Keller, an Educational Consultant and EMI Advisor and Teacher Trainer at Fulbright Taiwan (Foundation for Scholarly Exchange), alongside Christopher, for a comprehensive English as a Medium of Instruction (EMI) classroom observation of my Beginning Strength and Conditioning course.

This experience served as a profound continuation of the pedagogical foundation I developed during the Fulbright Taiwan EMI Overseas Professional Training Workshop at Arizona State University. The immersive strategies acquired at ASU have been instrumental in shaping my bilingual teaching framework, and having Alexis—with her extensive background in teacher training—and Christopher here to evaluate its practical application was incredibly rewarding.

實務教學動態的深度檢視 (Evaluating Instructional Dynamics in Action)

Their nuanced feedback provided a crucial lens through which to assess the efficacy of several core pedagogical mechanics:

  • Pre-distributing instructional materials
  • Strategically positioning the instructor for optimal student engagement
  • Configuring effective group dynamics
  • Orchestrating a seamless instructional flow

Their collaborative presence not only validated the rigorous communicative strategies required in higher education physical instruction but also catalyzed a deeply constructive dialogue on fostering an inclusive yet academically demanding environment.

結語與致謝 (Conclusion and Acknowledgements)

I am immensely grateful for their dedicated mentorship and the actionable insights they shared, which will undoubtedly elevate the caliber of my future lectures and practical coaching demonstrations.

item.title: 2026 Functional Exercise Activity Design: Bridging Movement Science and Practice
item.description:
As an Adjunct Lecturer in the Department of Leisure and Recreation Management at Taipei City University of Science and Technology, I focus on transforming a passion for fitness into a scientifically grounded career. My teaching methodology bridges the gap between movement science and real-world functional application.

Foundational Movement, Functional Equipment, Activity Design!

2026 Functional Exercise Activity Design

Bridging the Gap Between Science and Application

In my course, 2026 Functional Exercise Activity Design, I guide students through the principles of functional movement, drawing inspiration from high-performance protocols like HYROX and the NSCA’s Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning. By integrating English as a Medium of Instruction (EMI) methodologies and active learning strategies like Think-Pair-Share and scaffolding, my approach ensures that future professionals don’t just memorize terms but deeply understand the biomechanics of multi-planar movement.

This instructional framework prepares students for advanced practice and coaching certifications, focusing on movement efficiency, velocity-based training, and the practical application of functional strength equipment.

Watch Course Description on YouTube

Core Pillars of My Instruction

The curriculum is built around three critical domains:

  1. Foundational Movement Science: We explore kinetic chains, bioenergetics, and biomechanics. It’s not just about naming muscles; it’s about understanding how the human body generates power across the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes during dynamic, real-world activities.
  2. Applied Functional Technique: From kettlebell swings and free weights to velocity-based training and cardiovascular intervals, students utilize a wide array of functional implements to refine their coaching and demonstration skills.
  3. Activity Design & Programming: This is where science becomes art. Students learn to design safe, effective functional programs for diverse goals—from strength-endurance to high-intensity functional training—and for populations ranging from athletic competitors to those seeking improved daily mobility.

Inside the Classroom: Practical Teaching Demonstrations

Translating Movement Science to Client Success

A proficient strength and conditioning coach must be able to analyze a client’s foundational movement patterns—such as the hinge, squat, push, pull, and carry—instantly. In this segment, I explain how to assess movement efficiency using functional tools like free weights. By deeply understanding kinetic linking, future instructors can provide precise verbal cues and drastically reduce the risk of client injury.

Watch on YouTube

Mastering the Functional Assessment and Framework

Success in functional training relies on identifying movement limitations and properly introducing equipment. This video captures how I teach students to conduct dynamic movement assessments and establish the foundational framework for safely integrating kettlebells and velocity-based metrics into a client’s routine.

Watch on YouTube

Long-Term Programming Strategy: Manipulating Variables for Functional Fitness

To prevent client plateaus and overtraining, professionals must master the art of periodization for functional fitness. Here, I illustrate how to strategically manipulate FITT-VP variables specifically for functional and HYROX-style conditioning, ensuring sustainable, long-term adaptations.

Watch on YouTube

The Golden Rules of Functional Adaptation

Generic workouts fail to produce movement proficiency. In this lecture highlight, I break down the core principles of functional training: Specificity, Overload, and Movement Quality. I place a strong emphasis on aligning energy systems and functional mechanics with a client’s unique health or performance goals.

Watch on YouTube

Professional Excellence & Certification

The ultimate goal of this methodology is to ensure students are ready to lead clients toward their functional goals with absolute confidence and scientific backing.

  • Instructional Focus: Meticulously aligned with NSCA-CSCS domains and advanced functional training standards.
  • Pedagogical Innovation: Integration of EMI active learning strategies and hands-on application with functional strength equipment.
  • Industry Expertise: Grounded in my experience as a PhD candidate and holder of NSCA-CSCS*D, ACSM-CEP, and ACSM-EP certifications.

item.title: 2026 Fall Beginning Strength and Conditioning: Bridging Science and Practice (EMI & Bilingual)
item.description:
As an Adjunct Lecturer (兼任講師) at National Taiwan Normal University (NTNU / 臺師大), I focus on transforming a passion for fitness into a scientifically grounded practice. My teaching methodology bridges the gap between exercise science and real-world application in the Beginning Strength and Conditioning (初階肌力與體能訓練) course.

To cultivate a diverse and international learning environment, this course is offered in two dedicated sessions:

  • 🕒 Friday 13:20 ~ 15:20 (EMI): English as a Medium of Instruction
  • 🕒 Friday 15:30 ~ 17:30 (Mandarin): Chinese Instruction

Foundational Science, Applied Technique, Program Design!

Course Teaching Methodology

Bridging the Gap Between Science and Application

In my course, Beginning Strength and Conditioning, I guide students through the “Gold Standard” of the industry—the NSCA’s Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning. My approach ensures that students don’t just memorize terms but truly understand the “why” behind the “how” of lifting and athletic performance.

This instructional video provides an overview of how the course is structured to prepare students with foundational knowledge in anatomical adaptations, biomechanics, and proper lifting mechanics.

Watch Course Description on YouTube

Core Pillars of My Instruction

Based on my teaching demonstration, the curriculum is built around three critical domains, delivered effectively in both English and Chinese:

  1. Foundational Science: We explore anatomy, bioenergetics, and biomechanics. It’s not just about naming muscles; it’s about understanding how the human body generates power and adapts to physical stress.
  2. Applied Technique: From core stability exercises to foundational barbell lifts (squat, hinge, push, pull) and cardiovascular protocols, students practice techniques outlined in our resources to refine their lifting and coaching skills.
  3. Program Design: This is where science becomes art. Students learn to design safe, effective programs for diverse goals—from hypertrophy to strength and aerobic endurance.

Inside the Classroom: Practical Teaching Demonstrations

Translating Movement Science to Lifting Success

A proficient practitioner must be able to analyze posture and movement efficiency instantly. In this segment, I explain how to utilize the three planes of motion (sagittal, frontal, and transverse) and varying lever systems in practical scenarios. By deeply understanding concentric, eccentric, and isometric contractions, students can provide precise verbal cues and drastically reduce the risk of injury.

(Note: In the EMI session, these cues are taught using international standard terminology to prepare students for global contexts.)

Watch on YouTube

Mastering the Initial Framework of Strength Training

Success in strength and conditioning relies on proper assessment and systematic progression. This video captures how I teach students to establish the foundational framework for both their aerobic and resistance training routines.

Watch on YouTube

Long-Term Programming Strategy: The GAS Model

To prevent plateaus and overtraining, one must master the art of periodization. Here, I introduce the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) to illustrate how the human body responds to physiological stress. Students learn to strategically manipulate FITT-VP variables to create sustainable, long-term adaptations.

Watch on YouTube

The Golden Rules of Physiological Adaptation

Generic workouts fail to produce specific results. In this lecture highlight, I break down the three non-negotiable rules of training: Specificity, Overload, and Progression. I place a strong emphasis on the Principle of Specificity, teaching students how to select exercises and energy systems that directly align with unique health or performance goals.

Watch on YouTube

Professional Excellence & Global Readiness

The ultimate goal of this methodology is to ensure students are equipped with world-class strength and conditioning knowledge, ready to apply these principles safely and effectively.

  • Bilingual Advantage: Teaching through both EMI and Mandarin equips NTNU students with local adaptability and international competitiveness.
  • Instructional Focus: Meticulously aligned with NSCA evidence-based guidelines.
  • Industry Expertise: Grounded in my experience as a PhD candidate and holder of NSCA-CSCS*D and ACSM-CEP certifications.
